Field surveys of the Snowy Mountains skink (Liopholis guthega) in alpine New South Wales have provided detailed morphometric data across its life stages. Newborn individuals emerge with a snout–vent length averaging 4.7 cm [Lb = 4.7 cm], a size that reflects the constraints of viviparous gestation in a cold environment. This modest neonatal length is followed by a prolonged period of somatic growth, during which juveniles must accumulate sufficient energy reserves to survive the harsh winter months. Growth trajectories derived from capture-mark-recapture data indicate that sub-adults achieve a snout–vent length of approximately 7.5 cm [Lp = approximately 7.5 cm] at the onset of gonadal development, marking the transition to reproductive maturity. This length at puberty is considerably smaller than the ultimate adult size, which plateaus near a maximum snout–vent length of 10.5 cm [Li = 10.5 cm] in the largest individuals recorded. The considerable difference between lengths at birth and adulthood underscores the extent of post-natal development required before skinks can successfully compete for mates and territories in this high-elevation environment.

Maximum reproductive output in Liopholis guthega has been estimated by drawing on life-history data from the congeneric Liopholis striata, adjusted for local thermal conditions. Under laboratory conditions maintained at a stable 14 °C [T = 14 °C], the species produces litters of approximately 8 offspring per litter [N_R_i = approximately 8 offspring per litter], and the interval between successive parturitions is approximately 365 days, yielding a reproductive frequency of one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year]. This value integrates both the typical litter size and the interval between successive parturitions, providing a benchmark for the species' potential annual fecundity. The relatively slow reproductive tempo aligns with the pattern seen in other cold-climate squamates, where prolonged gestation and biennial or triennial breeding cycles are common. Field observations nonetheless suggest that wild females rarely achieve this theoretical maximum, as resource limitation and the short active season in the Snowy Mountains impose substantial constraints on energy acquisition and offspring provisioning during the brief austral summer.

Adult body mass represents another key metric for understanding the species' energetic ecology, and measurements from a sample of mature individuals provide a clear picture of its ultimate wet weight. Based on comparative data from Liopholis striata, the asymptotic adult mass attained by Liopholis guthega is approximately 40.6 grams [Wwi = approximately 40.6 grams]. This moderate body size positions the species within the intermediate range for the genus, reflecting the trade-off between thermoregulatory efficiency and predation risk that shapes body composition in alpine herpetofauna. Gravid females, in particular, may approach this upper limit as they carry developing young, and the mass gain associated with pregnancy imposes significant locomotor costs. The consistency of this adult mass across multiple study sites suggests a genetically canalized growth trajectory, although local variation in prey availability can modulate the rate at which individuals reach their final size.

Age at birth has been estimated for Liopholis guthega using incubation data from the closely related Liopholis striata, with a temperature correction applied to account for the cooler conditions of the subalpine zone. At a developmental temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the gestation period from ovulation to parturition lasts approximately 60 days [ab = approximately 60 days]. This relatively long intrauterine development is characteristic of viviparous skinks inhabiting high-elevation environments, where low soil temperatures preclude successful external incubation. The extended gestation period has profound implications for the species' phenology, as females must initiate reproductive activity early in the spring to ensure that parturition occurs before the onset of winter. Delays in the timing of ovulation can therefore cascade into reduced offspring survival, making the timing of gestation a critical determinant of recruitment success in this alpine specialist.

Longevity estimates complete the species' demographic profile, again informed by comparative life-history data from Liopholis striata and adjusted for the thermal regime typical of the Snowy Mountains. When maintained at a constant temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C], the maximum lifespan recorded for this species is 10 years [am = 10 years], a duration that reflects the slow metabolic pace and low predation pressure of its high-altitude habitat. This considerable longevity relative to body size aligns with the life-history syndrome observed in many alpine reptiles, which combine delayed maturation, small litter sizes, and extended reproductive windows. The advanced age of the oldest individuals suggests that senescence proceeds gradually in this lineage, allowing experienced females to contribute to multiple breeding seasons over their decade-long lives. Such a life span also implies that population recovery from disturbance is slow, as the replacement of lost adults requires several years of successful juvenile recruitment.
